prompt: A plant needs a new maintenance technician posting by Friday, but there is no current job description. What should the PHR take from a job analysis before the posting goes live?

Last year's ratings of technicians in other plants
Personality labels taken from last year's top performers

distractorExplanations.d: Trait lists of 'top people' study persons, not the job, and invite non-job-related hiring screens.

prompt: A store director wants to hire only White clerks because 'our shoppers prefer it.' How should the PHR treat that request under Title VII?

options.text: Allow it as a race BFOQ based on customer preference
Allow an age cap if it would cut new-hire training cost
Refuse it; race has no BFOQ and preference is not a defense

explanation: Title VII permits no BFOQ for race or color. Customer preference is not a lawful basis for excluding a protected group. distractorExplanations.d: Confuses BFOQ (using a protected trait openly) with the business-necessity defense used after a neutral practice shows impact.

prompt: A written screen's Hispanic pass rate is 60% of the White pass rate. What should the PHR do first under the Uniform Guidelines (UGESP)?

prompt: Applicants take the same cognitive screen two weeks apart and their rank order changes sharply. What does that reliability problem mean for hiring decisions?

Scores are unstable, so the rank order cannot be trusted

explanation: Reliability is score consistency. If rank order jumps on retest, you cannot trust who scored 'higher' and should not use the tool as a hurdle. distractorExplanations.a: Wrong construct is a validity problem; reliability asks whether the measure is consistent, not whether it is the right trait.
distractorExplanations.c: Adverse impact is about group pass-rate gaps; bouncing scores are a consistency issue, not a four-fifths finding.

prompt: A finger is cleaned, bandaged, and the employee returns to full duty the same shift. No prescription, stitches, or lost time. Is this OSHA-recordable for a covered employer?

options.text: Yes; any visible blood on a tool automatically becomes an OSHA recordable case under Part 1904
Yes; every workers' compensation claim, even if later denied, must appear on the 300 log
Yes; adhesive bandages count as medical treatment beyond first aid under OSHA recordkeeping rules
Generally no; cleaning and a bandage without days away, restriction, or treatment beyond first aid stays first aid

explanation: OSHA lists cleaning wounds and using bandages as first aid. First aid alone, with no days away, restricted work, job transfer, or medical treatment beyond first aid, is not recordable. Blood on a tool, a WC claim, or a bandage does not by itself convert the case. Contrast this with prescription medication, stitches, or lost time, which typically do.

distractorExplanations.a: Blood exposure on equipment is not an automatic 300-log trigger; apply the recording criteria.
distractorExplanations.b: Workers' comp and OSHA recordkeeping use different tests; a WC filing does not force a 300 entry.
distractorExplanations.c: Bandages are on OSHA's first-aid list, not medical treatment beyond first aid.

prompt: Outside counsel is redlining the employee handbook in an at-will state. Which disclaimer best reduces implied-contract risk?

options.text: Employment is promised for at least 12 months after the employee signs the acknowledgment
Discipline will follow every numbered step in the progressive-discipline chart in every case
The handbook is not a contract; employment is at-will and the company may revise policies
Policies change only when a majority of employees vote to accept the revision

explanation: Handbooks can create implied contracts if they guarantee tenure or lock the employer into every listed process. A clear at-will statement, a 'not a contract' disclaimer, and a reserved right to change policies are the usual PHR controls. Promising a year of work, promising every discipline step, or requiring an employee vote does the opposite.

distractorExplanations.a: A one-year guarantee is a term contract, which undercuts at-will instead of preserving it.
distractorExplanations.b: Mandatory step charts are a classic implied-contract hook that limits discharge discretion.
distractorExplanations.d: Requiring an employee vote to change rules treats the handbook like a bargained contract.

prompt: Operations wants a 40-page overtime-approval SOP copied into the employee handbook 'so nobody can say they were not told.' What is the better PHR design?

options.text: Keep a short handbook rule and house the detailed SOP in a manager policy you can update
Paste every operational SOP into the handbook so the acknowledgment covers each procedure
Replace the handbook with Slack pins, which never create handbook-contract risk
Publish overtime rules only inside a union contract, even at a nonunion site

explanation: The handbook is the employee-facing summary of rules and disclaimers. Long manager SOPs belong in a policy/procedure library so operations can revise workflows without implying that every checklist is a contractual right. A receipt acknowledgment still covers the handbook rule. Slack pins are still communications that can create expectations, and a nonunion site has no CBA to hide procedures in.

distractorExplanations.b: Stuffing SOPs into the handbook bloats it and makes each revision look like a bargained term.
distractorExplanations.c: Informal chat posts can still create policy promises; they are not a safe substitute handbook.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonunion employer has no union contract vehicle; that answer invents a CBA that does not exist.

prompt: A supervisor emails the whole shift a scanned doctor's note describing an employee's lifting limits 'so everyone can help.' What should HR do?

options.text: File the doctor's note in the ordinary personnel file so any future supervisor can open it
Add the diagnosis to the OSHA 300A annual posting so coworkers see why the job was modified
Forward the doctor's note to payroll to store with Forms I-9, because leave tracking sits with hire forms
Move it into a confidential medical file, separate from personnel, and limit access to need-to-know

explanation: ADA (and related privacy practice) requires that employee medical information be collected on a need-to-know basis and kept in a confidential medical file separate from the personnel file. A team-wide email of a doctor's note is a disclosure. Coworkers may need a functional restriction ('no lifts over 20 pounds'), not the diagnosis or the scan.

distractorExplanations.a: The personnel file is too broadly available; medical notes do not belong there.
distractorExplanations.b: The 300A summary is an injury-count poster, not a place to publish a coworker's diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.c: I-9 files are for employment-eligibility forms, not medical notes or FMLA clinical detail.

prompt: Benefits asks HR to email a spreadsheet of employee Social Security numbers to a new broker 'to speed the census.' What is the right privacy response?

options.text: Send the file if the spreadsheet name includes the word confidential
CC the entire leadership team so executives share responsibility for the transfer
Refuse the open email; send only needed fields through a secure channel to a vetted vendor
Post the census on the intranet so employees can self-correct SSNs before the broker sees them

explanation: SSNs are high-risk personal data. PHR practice is minimum necessary: confirm the broker is under contract, use a secure transfer, and send only the fields the census actually requires. A 'confidential' filename, a wider CC list, or an intranet post increases exposure instead of reducing it and can trigger state breach-notice duties if the file is misdirected.

distractorExplanations.a: A filename label does not encrypt the attachment or stop a misaddressed email from being a breach.
distractorExplanations.b: Copying more executives multiplies inboxes that hold SSNs; it does not transfer legal risk away from HR.
distractorExplanations.d: Posting SSNs internally is a broadcast, not a safeguard, and far exceeds need-to-know.

prompt: A line manager wants PDFs of every direct report's full personnel file for 'career talks,' including investigation memos and I-9 copies. What should HR release?

options.text: The entire personnel file; any supervisor of record is entitled to every document stored in that file
Job-related performance documents on a need-to-know basis, not investigations, medical notes, or I-9s
I-9 copies and medical notes, but withhold performance reviews as too sensitive for line managers
The full PDFs to the manager's personal email so the files can be read off-network at home

explanation: Personnel information is disclosed on a need-to-know basis. A supervisor may see current performance, goals, and job history needed to coach. Investigation files, medical information, and I-9s serve other legal purposes and are not career-talk material. Emailing full files to a personal account also loses custody of sensitive records.

distractorExplanations.a: Supervisor status is not a master key to investigations, medical data, or I-9s.
distractorExplanations.c: That pair is backwards: performance is what the manager needs; I-9s and medical notes are not.
distractorExplanations.d: Personal email takes records outside employer systems and heightens a privacy incident.
